title: Andy Burnham to address social care, youth unemployment and devolution
description: The source said: "He has the courage to fix the most difficult issues that have been ignored for years and seen as impossible to resolve. He doesn't a
body: The source said: "He has the courage to fix the most difficult issues that have been ignored for years and seen as impossible to resolve. He doesn't accept that they are. They can't be ignored any longer."The prime minister is determined to show that governments can make people's lives better if they choose to. He wants to get Britain believing again."Unlike the NHS, social care is not free at the point of use, and people with savings worth more than £23,250 are not entitled to help with the cost of care from their local council.Burnham would not be the first leader in recent years to pledge to address the issue of adult social care. In 2019, in his first speech as prime minister, Boris Johnson said the Conservative Party would "fix the crisis in social care once and for all".Five years later in July 2024, Keir Starmer faced criticism when Labour scrapped plans for an £86,000 cap on the amount anyone in England would need to spend on their personal care over their lifetime. Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey, who has pushed for social care reform, said on Saturday:  "This has to be the start of a real effort to end the social care catastrophe."He added: "I'll fight to ensure family carers aren't forgotten. We need cross-party consensus, and I hope the PM's door is open."Burnham responded to Sir Ed on X, writing: "It most certainly is, Ed. Let's work together to find some common ground."Kevin Hollinrake, chairman of the Conservative Party, said: "Where's the money coming from, Andy? We're all dying to know."It is all well and good for the prime minister to promise to fix the issues facing our country, but how is he going to pay for them?"In the first week of his premiership, Burnham has pledged to end rough sleeping in England, cut VAT from domestic electricity bills in the current financial year, and reduce the cap on bus fares outside of London from £3 to £2 from January.His government also announced it would cut business rates for pubs, clubs, and live music venues in England by 20% from April.

title: Nethy Bridge: Residents allowed to return after evacuation from Cairngorms wildfire
description: Residents of the village of Nethy Bridge, near the wildfire that has been burning in the Cairngorms, have been told they can return to their homes aft
body: Residents of the village of Nethy Bridge, near the wildfire that has been burning in the Cairngorms, have been told they can return to their homes after being evacuated on Friday night.The fire was declared a major incident due to a change in weather, but that has now been stood down by Police Scotland.First Minister John Swinney said the government and emergency services will continue to treat the blaze with the utmost seriousness until the last flames are out.Locals have criticised the handling of the wildfire, which has been burning for 10 days, saying the move to declare it a major incident came too late and the government had been slow in scaling up their response.In a statement on Saturday night, Police Scotland said "after an extensive multi-agency response to a large fire within Cairngorms National Park, residents of Nethy Bridge are being advised that they can now return to their properties".Police Scotland's deputy assistant chief officer, Kenny Barbour, said the decision to stand down the major incident followed a detailed assessment by emergency responders. He added in a statement: "The extensive work carried out over recent days, including the creation of effective fire breaks, has significantly reduced the risk to nearby communities, allowing evacuated residents to safely return home."Supt Judy Hill added that the "ongoing multi agency response remains a high priority, with significant partnership resources and volunteers working tirelessly and in challenging circumstances, to support our efforts to extinguish the fires".Firefighters will continue to maintain a significant operational presence until the incident is safely concluded, with 75 remaining on the ground on Saturday, police said. At a meeting of the Scottish government's resilience room on Saturday evening, the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service said there had been "good progress" in strengthening fire breaks to protect residential areas and said the number of fire hot spots was reducing.First Minister John Swinney welcomed the lifting of the evacuation notice but stressed that "the Scottish Government, the emergency services and all relevant authorities will continue to treat this wildfire, as has been the case since its onset, with the utmost seriousness and necessary resources until the last flames are out."Nethy Bridge residents said there had not been enough communication from the government about the wildfire, and also criticised the time that was taken to declare it a major incident.Nethy Bridge community council leader Sandy McCook earlier said too many decisions had been "taken from Edinburgh", while local resident John McGlinchey said the evacuation was "just not organised properly".The Cabinet Secretary for Justice, Neil Gray, said: "Throughout this significant incident, the government and the emergency services have given everything to ensuring that the fire is being addressed."The fire broke out near the village of Glenmore on Wednesday last week, and led to residents and campsites being evacuated.It covered about six square kilometres of heather and small trees at its height, with more than 500 firefighters tackling it.In an update on Saturday morning, Police Scotland said residents in a small area of properties north-west of Dorback Lodge (Lain Thatchan) had also been evacuated as a precaution.Residents living in the affected areas and those impacted by the spread of smoke, including Aberdeenshire and Moray, have been advised to keep all windows and doors closed.

schema.headline: Nethy Bridge: Residents allowed to return after evacuation from Cairngorms wildfire

title: Anthony Joshua vs Kristian Prenga: Briton suffers two knockdowns in first round but wins in second
description: Anthony Joshua suffered two knockdowns - the first happening after just 20 seconds - before recovering to dramatically stop Kristian Prenga in the sec
body: Anthony Joshua suffered two knockdowns - the first happening after just 20 seconds - before recovering to dramatically stop Kristian Prenga in the second round of his comeback fight in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.The British heavyweight was fighting for the first time since surviving the December car crash in Nigeria that claimed the lives of his close friends Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele.He was sensationally rocked by a huge uppercut from underdog Prenga in the opening round, and then hit the canvas again later in the round.At that point he looked on the verge of one of the biggest shock defeats in heavyweight history, with the long-awaited Tyson Fury fight hanging by a thread.But Joshua produced one of the greatest escapes of his career, and now that fight is on.He unleashed his right hand in the second round, with the final shot sending Albanian Prenga crashing down and forcing the referee to halt the contest."It's more than punch power. That was spirit, that was Latz, that was Sina, that was the families. It hurts to even talk about it. It has been tough," Joshua, 36, said.He choked up and stepped away from the microphone, before adding: "It's my brothers. I don't want to talk about it."There had been speculation fellow Briton Fury might make a appearance despite insisting he would not attend.But the master of mind games stayed true to his word, with Fury nowhere to be seen barely 24 hours on from his own warm-up win over Mariusz Wach in Thailand."I respect everything he has done and everything that he has achieved, but as a fighting person, we're here now. I hope the fans will be in for a lovely treat," Joshua said about the prospect of fighting Fury.Contracts have been signed, but the venue and date for a fight more than a decade in the making are still unknown.This chaotic night, however, belonged to Joshua in a victory forged through adversity during the most difficult months of his life.Given the circumstances, this was never going to be a straightforward return for Joshua. Few, however, could have predicted the drama that unfolded inside six minutes.Joshua carried the names of Ghami and Ayodele on his chest and walked to the ring alongside his entire team in a quiet show of unity. The canvas carried their names too, alongside the words 'My Brother's Keeper'.His comeback could scarcely have begun in any worse fashion. Just 20 seconds in, a right uppercut from Prenga sent Joshua crashing to the canvas and stunned the arena.Joshua smiled as he climbed to his feet. Prenga, who arrived with 20 knockouts from his 20 victories but little profile even with boxing's hardcore followers, sensed an opportunity.Promoter Eddie Hearn barked instructions from ringside, while Joshua stablemate Oleksandr Usyk watched on with a look of concern.A left uppercut later in the round dumped Joshua on the canvas again. He was still unsteady at the start of the second round and appeared to be there for the taking, but Prenga surprisingly began to box off the back foot and let the Watford fighter off the hook.Joshua capitalised and using his years of experience - and perhaps the emotion - he drew Prenga on to a jab before uncorking a crushing right hand. More rights followed as Prenga collapsed to the canvas and the referee had seen enough.This was 35-year-old Prenga's second loss in his career.It was Joshua's first test against a recognised professional opponent since Daniel Dubois stopped him in September 2024.His only fight since had come against YouTuber-turned-boxer Jake Paul in December, 10 days before the fatal crash that left him injured.Joshua passed the Prenga test, but not in the manner anyone expected. It was not the destructive, free-flowing champion who once swept opponents aside.After defeating 46-year-old Wach in Pattaya, the question of whether Fury would show up to watch Joshua became a subplot of fight night.A Fury lookalike briefly fooled reporters when he stepped out of a taxi, while Fury's manager Spencer Brown insisted the 'Gypsy King' would be "there in spirit".The fight between two of the most recognisable names in British boxing is understood to have been agreed for November.Neither man is at the peak of his powers, but while the commercial appeal remains strong, Joshua's struggles are likely to leave Fury a clear favourite.The bout is expected to stream on Netflix. British fans are hoping for a homecoming event, but it is understood Saudi organisers and broadcasters favour a venue in the United States to cater for American audiences."We've signed the contract. Everything is done," Hearn said."But tonight wasn't about Tyson Fury. It was about the strength Anthony Joshua has shown just to be here."No-one knows what he's been through over the last seven months. When he went down in the first round, I thought he'd come back too soon."

schema.headline: Anthony Joshua vs Kristian Prenga: Briton suffers two knockdowns in first round but wins in second

title: What a week's work experience taught these Year 10s about their futures
description: When Kelsey first arrived at secondary school, she said she wanted to be almost anywhere else but there.She struggled with friendships, clashed with t
body: When Kelsey first arrived at secondary school, she said she wanted to be almost anywhere else but there.She struggled with friendships, clashed with teachers and often tried to avoid coming into school.But after a week's work experience placement at Whipsnade Zoo, in Bedfordshire, her outlook could not be more different.She said it made her a "completely different person" - more confident, with a "good group of friends" and a greater sense of purpose about where her education could lead her.Children across the UK are strongly encouraged to do work experience while at school. In England, the government published new legal guidance in June for schools to deliver two weeks of "in-person and immersive" work experience in future, one between Year 7 and Year 9, and one between Years 10 and 11.But not all work experience placements are equal, and finding the right one can be tricky.Organisations like the Sutton Trust and the Social Mobility Foundation said some students could be limited by the availability of placements in their area, or a lack of family connections with local employers.BBC News spoke to three Year 10 pupils, one year ahead of their final GCSE exams, about how they decided what areas of work they were interested in, their experiences of trying to find the right placement, and what it taught them about their future education and ultimate career goals.Erica Holt-White, research and policy manager at the Sutton Trust, said the experiences of these students, and thousands of others like them, show why meaningful work experience can be so beneficial.It can be particularly valuable for young people who do not have family or friends working in the industries they are interested in."It gives them exposure to professional environments and the chance to meet people in careers they might otherwise never encounter," she said.But access to those opportunities remains unequal, according to Sarah Atkinson, chief executive of the Social Mobility Foundation."Many schools now ask students to find placements themselves," she said."That creates significant inequalities, because young people without family or professional networks are far more likely either to miss out altogether, or to end up in placements that aren't relevant to their ambitions."Both said work experience does not need to lead directly to a future career to be valuable.For Kelsey, the lessons from Whipsnade Zoo continue to shape both her ambitions and her approach to education.Her advice to younger pupils is simple."Take the opportunity when it's offered - talk to people, ask questions and enjoy it because you'll learn far more than you expect."

schema.headline: What a week's work experience taught these Year 10s about their futures

title: Peterborough farm's delight after six white owlets found nesting
description: Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The owlets were ringed on Thursday by Simon DudhillByShariqua AhmedCambridgeA nest of six barn owlets has br
body: Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The owlets were ringed on Thursday by Simon DudhillByShariqua AhmedCambridgeA nest of six barn owlets has brought good news to a farm after a challenging period.The fluffy birds - which are estimated to be between 40 to 50 days old - were discovered at Moor Farm, near Peterborough, and were ringed on Thursday as part of ongoing conservation work.Judith Jacobs, the farm's owner, said the owlets were thriving and had lifted spirits after the farm was the target of six suspected arson attacks this summer.Simon Dudhill, who monitors the birds for Peterborough City Council's barn owl recovery scheme, said finding six owlets sharing a nest was "exceptionally good" and was the largest brood he had encountered in 2026.He added he had ringed more than 260 owlets in Cambridgeshire this year. Each bird from Moor Farm was fitted with a metal ring carrying a unique identification number issued by the British Trust for Ornithology. The ring's details allow conservationists to track individual birds and provides information about their movements. Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, Simon Dudhill said finding six owlets together was "exceptionally good"Jacobs said: "It's very exciting as we had none last year. We try and encourage wildlife as much as we can. "We have created a lot of hunting paths for the owls away from the main road, so they can hunt safely, because the biggest predators for barn owls are cars."She said the six owlets, which include three females and three males, are each about three days apart in age."Simon measured the length of their fourth feather, which tells their age, and from the colour of their feathers, if they are spotty they are females and the non-spotty ones are males," she added. Image source, Robert JacobsImage caption, The six owlets are each about three days apart in age and include three males and three femalesDudhill, who works for the Wildlife Conservation Partnership, external, said 2026 had been a much stronger breeding year for barn owls."I have ringed quite a few groups of five and four owlets this year. But this is the first  brood of six I have found," he added."Over the last couple of years, we have seen a decline in the number of babies but not adult barn owls. "Last year we found a lot of adults in boxes but they did not breed. This is all related to food. If there isn't enough food around, then they don't breed. "This year has been completely different. I personally found barn owl numbers have increased dramatically. But there are still some areas in Cambridgeshire that have not found as many babies as I have," he said. Despite monitoring barn owls for 15 years, Dudhill said the experience "never gets boring"."When you open a box, you have one or two or three little faces looking at you. It's just as exciting now as the first time I opened a box," he added. Do you have a story suggestion for Peterborough? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

title: Rental searches for pet friendly properties drop after law change
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentRightmove searches for rental properties that allow pets have plummeted since law changes gave
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentRightmove searches for rental properties that allow pets have plummeted since law changes gave renters more rights.Following the introduction of the new rules, pet searches dropped by more than 50% in May and June compared with a year earlier.Landlords in England cannot unreasonably refuse pets in their properties under changes made in May in the Renters' Rights Act.But agents say some renters wrongly believe permission to have a pet is guaranteed, and landlords say some homes remain unsuitable for multiple pets or large dogs."Landlords must consider requests fairly and cannot unreasonably refuse them, but they can still decline where there is a valid reason," said Megan Eighteen, immediate past president of lettings agents trade body ARLA Propertymark.She said there was plenty of "potential for misunderstanding", among tenants about pet-friendly properties.Power shift over petsThe Rightmove data suggests that fewer tenants are proactively filtering for pet-friendly properties when searching for a home. While pets remain the most common searched-for term overall - ahead of gardens, garages and furnishings, the lead at the top is shrinking.Renter searches for properties that allow pets fell by 54% in May and 52% in June compared with the same months a year earlier, according to the figures shared with the BBC. Falls had accelerated through this year, as the changes got closer and were then introduced.Marc von Grundherr, director of agency Benham and Reeves, said some tenants have only disclosed a pet after signing their tenancy agreement, while others have been discovered during property inspections."The reality is that tenants now understand the balance of power has shifted. Landlords can no longer rely on a blanket 'no pets' policy to deter applications and should instead expect conversations around pet ownership to arise much later in the letting process," he said.Now, in England, landlords may still be able to refuse a pet if another tenant has an allergy, the property is too small for a large pet or several pets, the pet is illegal, or the landlord is a leaseholder and the freeholder does not allow pets.Before the rules changed, Eve Williamson had to give up her American Bulldog, Khan, or face eviction from her home - despite having previously had a dog in the property.The 41-year-old former hairdresser, from London, described the experience as awful, especially as Khan had brought comfort while she gave full-time care to her mum."Life can get tough, but pets bring unconditional love," she said. "They're family."Image source, Eve WilliamsonImage caption, Eve had to give up her dog - Khan - or face evictionKhan has since been happily re-homed, and Eve said she was delighted with the law change. Katie Smith, 29, from Swindon, has two cats - Pumpkin and Pippin - in her rental home. The new mum said the family had shared "wonderful moments" with pets, which would also teach children about life and death.But she said the choice of places to rent still dropped sharply on property portals when pets were part of the equation."Landlords should give them a chance," she said. Yet, even under the new rules, landlords were finding excuses to refuse potential tenants with pets, according to Russell Hunt, founder of Pets Lets, which matches clients with pet-friendly rentals.Image source, Russell HuntImage caption, Russell Hunt said landlords should consider each pet request on its meritsHe lives with a Basset Beagle cross, called Biscuit, and his three teenagers, who he jokes are more disruptive than the dog.He said pet CVs should be used and landlords should consider the circumstances more carefully, such as older dogs being calmer and sleeping more, rather than simply ruling out tenants with large or multiple pets. Cost to landlordsRepresentatives for landlords say they understand the importance of companionship that pets offer to tenants, but they can still face costly damage."Many landlords have legitimate concerns about the risk that some irresponsible pet owners pose to rental properties, or that some owners may try to keep pets in properties that are not appropriate for animals," said Chris Norris, chief policy officer at the National Residential Landlords Association.He said that landlords faced issues including: No power to compel tenants to take out insuranceNo legal right to request an additional depositA burden of costs should a pet cause damage to a propertyLesley Horton, the UK's chief property ombudsman said that landlords should not be levying pet surcharges as this fell outside permitted fees for issues such as late payments or lost key replacements.However, a landlord could make deductions from the tenancy deposit at the end of the tenancy for proven pet-related damage.Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell. Get in touchAre you affected by the issues raised in this story?

title: Tour de France 2026: Tadej Pogacar set for record fifth win
description: Tadej Pogacar is set to secure a record-equalling fifth Tour de France after a dramatic stage 20 saw Ecuador's Richard Carapaz clinch victory on Alpe
body: Tadej Pogacar is set to secure a record-equalling fifth Tour de France after a dramatic stage 20 saw Ecuador's Richard Carapaz clinch victory on Alpe d'Huez as Sepp Kuss crashed twice while leading in the last few kilometres.If Pogacar avoids a race-ending crash on Sunday's final stage to Paris, in which the overall standings are traditionally not contested, he will become the joint-most successful rider in the Tour's history alongside Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain.Pogacar, 27, of UAE Team Emirates-XRG, finished the three-week Grand Tour's 'queen' stage in fourth place after helping his 22-year-old Mexican team-mate Isaac del Toro provisionally seal third place on the overall podium and the young rider classification's white jersey. The pair crossed the line together with their arms around each other's shoulders after Pogacar paced a suffering Del Toro up the final climb.Pogacar will claim his fifth overall yellow jersey in Paris by six minutes and 26 seconds over Belgium's Remco Evenepoel of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, after Evenepoel finished the stage in second, 26 seconds behind Carapaz, after a late charge."I did my best to help Isaac," said Pogacar afterwards. "Massive respect for what all the guys have been doing in the past three weeks. I finally experienced [being a domestique] myself and I already before appreciate [the] work of team-mates, but now it's like another level."It was goosebumps [as we crossed the line together]. [It] was fantastic and one for the memories."On his future, he added: "I definitely will not be doing this for too much [of a] long time, I think. Isaac showed great potential, but we don't put any pressure yet on Isaac." Race organisers ASO announced during the stage that Sunday's finale will have its distance reduced from 133km to 89km after the redirection of emergency services to help tackle devastating wildfires in the south-west of the country. Traditionally, the final stage sees the sport's sprinters battle for the line on the famous Champs Elysees cobbles, but a new section over Montmartre allows riders with more sustained power the potential to steal a breakaway win.The most demanding stage of the whole race was left to the penultimate day, in which riders had to climb 5,450 metres across three hors category climbs covering 170.9km to finish in the iconic Alpe d'Huez ski-resort for a second time in two days. American Kuss of Visma-Lease a Bike was part a large early breakaway which contained riders looking for a stage win, and attacked alone with about 25km to go.The 31-year-old looked to have found the strength which helped him win the Vuelta a Espana in 2023 and seemed set to hold on to a slender lead for victory. But the often unflappable Kuss was on the ragged edge and crashed coming out of a tunnel approaching Alpe d'Huez town. He maintained his lead, but soon after crashed again on a right-hand corner after getting his line wrong, his rear wheel sliding on dust at the edge of the road before coming to a stop, half off his bike and leaning into safety netting which prevented him from falling down a sheer drop.The tenacious Carapaz, of EF Education-Easypost, swept past Kuss and into the lead - the 2019 Giro d'Italia winner, eventually taking his second stage win in three days and also securing victory in the king of the mountains competition."[I was] not really scared," Kuss told TNT Sports afterwards. "I was just annoyed because we drove down it this morning and I looked at that corner and thought: 'Ah that's a pretty descent corner, no problem in the race,' so I took it pretty full-on. "It was a bit more of a corner than I expected. My wife won't let me race my bike anymore - she always tells me not take risks on the downhills, but you've got to have a little adrenaline rush every once in a while."Typically, on a stage such as this one in the French Alps, Pogacar would be expected to deliver yet another masterclass but he held back to help Del Toro, who at one point was starting to struggle on the Col du Galibier, to defend his white jersey and third place overall from French sensation Paul Seixas of Decathlon CMA-CGM.The 19-year-old Seixas finally ran out of energy on the final mountain of the race and is set to finish fourth in the general classification, 11 minutes and 56 seconds down on Pogacar's overall time.Britain's Tom Pidcock of Pinarello-Q36.5 finished the stage 16th, nine minutes and three seconds down, and will finish ninth overall in the GC.Denmark's Mads Pedersen of Lidl-Trek will win the green points jersey in Paris on Sunday just by finishing as he leads Belgium's Jasper Philipsen of Alpecin-Premier Tech by an uncatchable 82 points. title: Hungarian Grand Prix: Lando Norris cautious despite pole as qualifying 'falls apart' for Lewis Hamilton
description: Lando Norris took his first grand prix pole position of the year in Hungary but is cautious about whether he can follow it up with his first victory a
body: Lando Norris took his first grand prix pole position of the year in Hungary but is cautious about whether he can follow it up with his first victory as world champion.Perhaps the McLaren driver was casting his mind back to Miami in early May, when he was leading towards the end of the first stint of the race, only for his team to make a strategic misstep and allow Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli to sneak in for a win."You can't just rely on one good qualifying, so I need a good race tomorrow," Norris said."Then we obviously have a nice summer break, but after that we need to try and repeat it several more times."We've been working hard. We know we've been on the back foot, but we're making progress and today certainly shows that."Much of the attention at the Hungarian Grand Prix has been on the massive upgrade made by Aston Martin on their recalcitrant car, which has provided the troubled team with a major step forward and allowed Fernando Alonso to escape the first qualifying session for the first time all season.That meant McLaren's own upgrade went under the radar somewhat, but it has been effective.Still, team principal Andrea Stella, while expressing his satisfaction that the upgrades had enabled them to engage in a fight for pole they did not expect, said Norris' pole was an "overachievement".McLaren's own good execution of qualifying was one factor, he said, in addition to  an under-performance from Ferrari, and perhaps even Antonelli and Mercedes.Ferrari came into Hungary as most people's favourite, including McLaren's, on the basis that their car is the fastest in the corners, but it lacks engine performance, and this is one of the least power-sensitive tracks on the calendar.Lewis Hamilton was fastest after the first runs in the final part of qualifying but did not improve on his final lap. Shortly after completing it, he blocked Norris' team-mate Oscar Piastri and the stewards imposed a three-place grid penalty.Ferrari boss Frederic Vasseur said the team took responsibility for that because they did not warn Hamilton in time.The seven-time world champion later posted on Instagram:, external "Sometimes you just can't catch a break. Another weekend when I've been feeling great throughout all the sessions, but then it just falls apart."Referencing penalties he had been given in the previous two races in Britain and Belgium, Hamilton added: "I always do my best to keep positive - sport is always about the highs and lows, but it's also in the margins."Every point counts and you have to seize every opportunity. After three penalties in three weekends, it's becoming difficult to hang on to that positivity. "Still, I won't let the setbacks take away from the progress we've been making as a team. With the pace we have, I'm hopeful we can get something out of the race tomorrow."For all that Ferrari have been quick, Norris and McLaren have also looked in good shape all weekend. And, at least on this circuit, they have vaulted right to the front, into a position that had been familiar for the past two seasons but not so in 2026.While sat with Ferrari's Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, Norris said: "I knew the pace was certainly there. It has been all weekend. Even though these guys have been insanely fast, I knew I'd been driving very well, I'd been consistent, and I knew the car had potential. "We also had the upgrades this weekend, and it doesn't feel that different, but it certainly seems to be going a little bit quicker, and that's always a good thing." Overtaking is expected to be especially difficult around the Hungaroring this year. In Miami an excess of caution on McLaren's part about the potential of rain allowed Mercedes to pit Antonelli before Norris and leap into the lead.Norris' pole provides an opportunity to make amends for that - if he can keep Leclerc behind on the run to the first corner.After winning two consecutive constructors' titles in 2024 and 2025, as well as Norris' drivers' championship last year, McLaren have not had a great season at the start of this new regulation cycle.Securing the title against a late-season onslaught from Max Verstappen and Red Bull put them behind on designing this year's car, and they took some missteps on aerodynamic philosophy that only became fully understood after the first handful of races.An upgrade package introduced by McLaren this weekend, their first since Miami, is the fruit of work aimed at correcting course, and the first signs are positive.They have also struggled to get on top of the operation of the new Mercedes engine, feeling for the first time that they were suffering for not being a works partner of a manufacturer."It's just nice to be on pole," said Norris, who had also shown competitive pace in Belgium last weekend but was denied a good result by a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding the permitted number of engine parts, and then by bad luck with the timing of a safety car."I have felt good all weekend. The last few weekends, honestly, I felt pretty good and it's been nice I continued my good feelings in the car."I had my money on Ferrari before the weekend and they have been insanely quick, but, come qualifying, we just seemed to take more of a step forward. I knew it was possible and that has been a good feeling - and one that I have missed for quite a while."As for his prospects in the race, Norris alluded to strong performances from the Mercedes and Ferrari drivers on the race-simulation runs in Friday practice when he said: "The race pace on others looked very strong. It is always a bit tricky to know how things will go with a new car and new bits."Leclerc, though, felt Norris would certainly be in the fight, and both have some protection from Hamilton and Antonelli, both demoted by three-place penalties to fifth and seventh respectively."Lando seems to be very, very strong, so I'll say Lando [is favourite]," Leclerc said. "But if you look over the course of the season, Mercedes has always been up there, so I do not doubt that they'll all be in the fight as well."At Aston Martin there was at last some reason to feel positive after a dark time this season.So much had been expected of the team when design legend Adrian Newey joined in March last year, but a late start to their design process, combined with engine partner Honda falling well short of performance and - like McLaren - some errors in philosophy, have left them cemented at the back all year.In absolute terms, progressing beyond the first session for the first time all season, and lining up 16th, is nothing special. But to be able to compete with other teams, for pretty much the first time all year, was a major step.In percentage terms, this was not quite Aston Martin's best performance of the season - they were 0.012% closer to pole in Japan. But it is huge compared with where they have fallen since as others have developed their cars.There is a Honda engine upgrade to come for the next race after the summer break - of undefined size. More importantly, this has revitalised faith in Aston Martin's development capabilities after three years of upgrades that failed to deliver what the team expected."There is more potential to unlock in the car, but it's normal when you have such a big package," Alonso said."It was important for everyone in the team as it has been a tough period in both factories."Having the deficit that we had in terms of performance in the first half of the year and this package, it didn't change many positions, but it changed a lot the momentum of everyone in the factory."It's not any more that we are chasing something that we don't know. We know exactly what we are looking for and we know exactly the targets for the next package or the targets for next year. So that's for me the biggest change of this weekend."Whether it is enough for Alonso to decide to commit to another season behind the wheel remains to be seen.He turns 45 next week. He has said he still feels competitive - and continues to prove it. But he is no fan of the energy management required from this year's engines.He continues to profess his confidence that Newey and Honda will eventually produce the best car and engine. But, as he keeps repeating, the question is how long that will take, and whether it fits his timeline.As he said upon arriving in Hungary on Thursday: "It's not a problem with the competitiveness of the team. It's just a problem of whether Formula 1 gives me the adrenaline that I need to live."Alonso has a lot of thinking to do as he heads off on his summer break - his first as a father - next week.

schema.headline: Hungarian Grand Prix: Lando Norris cautious despite pole as qualifying 'falls apart' for Lewis Hamilton

title: What I learned when I reopened the Lockerbie bombing files
description: I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Officials inspect the wreck
body: I thought the Lockerbie bombing was a closed case until I started asking questionsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Officials inspect the wreckage of Pan Am flight 103 on 21 December 1988ByMyles BonnarBBC DisclosureI was only a year old when the UK's deadliest terror attack shocked the world.In December 1988, Pan Am flight 103 exploded over the Scottish town of Lockerbie, killing all 259 people on board as well as 11 on the ground.I was a teenager by the time Libyan intelligence officer Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was convicted of the bombing in 2001 and, when he later died, I thought that was largely the end of the story.It wasn't.The case still rumbles on and, later this year, a man suspected of making the bomb which blew up the plane, Abu Agila Masud, goes on trial in Washington DC.As part of a Radio 4 Intrigue podcast series, I had an opportunity to delve into this complex case with fresh eyes.The deeper I dug, the more complicated Lockerbie became and there have been times that I don't know what to believe.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Abdelbaset al-Megrahi was the only man convicted of the Lockerbie bombingJim Swire, on the other hand, is sure what he believes - and it is not the official story.His daughter Flora died in the bombing, but he is convinced that whoever killed her got away with mass murder.Swire believes Megrahi is innocent, even befriending the convicted bomber up until his death in 2012."The burning issue was to get to the truth," he says."Always has been, always will be and I will not shut up about what I know to be true."Swire's doggedness has made him a prominent voice but most of the Lockerbie victims' families don't agree that Megrahi's conviction was a miscarriage of justice - and the bomber’s own appeals against the verdict either failed or were abandoned.For Swire, the simplest explanation is that Iran was behind the attack - not Libya.The Lockerbie bombing came five months after 290 people were killed when an Iranian commercial airliner was shot down by a US battleship.Iran swore revenge and months later Pan Am flight 103 exploded on its way to New York.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Jim Swire's daughter Flora died in the Lockerbie bombingAnd there's more.Iran - much like they do now - used proxy militant groups to pursue their ends.Before the Lockerbie bombing, a militant cell based in Frankfurt, part of the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine - General Command (PFLP-GC), was foiled by German police.Police arrested suspects and seized explosive devices, concealed in radio cassette players, that were designed to trigger at altitude.The bomb that brought down Pan Am 103 was in a radio cassette player hidden inside a samsonite briefcase.Because of this, Swire believes the device that brought down Pan Am 103 was loaded at Frankfurt, and not Malta as the court had concluded.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A mock-up of the explosives-loaded Toshiba cassette recorder which blew up Pan Am Flight 103And, for Swire, this is only the tip of the iceberg.He also questions much of the evidence presented at the 2001 trial, discredits witnesses, and is extremely suspicious of the involvement of intelligence agencies - like MI5, MI6 and the CIA - in the aftermath of the bombing.Combine these suspicions with his all-consuming grief and you can see why Swire is such a force to be reckoned with on his quest for a truth he believes has been denied to him."Discovering the truth became my way of handling the consequences of the grief reaction," Swire says."And it was very tough for other people to understand that but that's just the way I'm made, I suppose."Intrigue: LockerbieOn 21 December 1988, a plane explodes over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing 270 people. Almost four decades on, there's fresh evidence. Who was really behind the bombing?Dick Marquise, who led the FBI's Lockerbie task force, says that in the early days of the case he too believed the PFLP-GC were the "number one suspect", but years of investigation found nothing to prove it."There was not one shred of evidence that could be taken to court and get a conviction," he says. "You couldn't do it. There was nothing."However, there are others, besides Swire, who still question the "official narrative" - including former CIA agent John Holt who also believes Iran was behind the bombing.Holt worked with Libyan intelligence assets in the 1980s and was the handler of double agent Abdul Majid Giaka, whose information became central to the investigation into the Lockerbie bombing.Holt now believes Giaka was a "BS artist" who was out for money and was feeding the CIA fake stories to get paid."I didn't think much of him at all," he says."He gave us some little tidbits about what was going on, but he never knew anything about the Pan Am bombing. And he knew a lot about Megrahi," Holt says.Holt believes the fact the CIA bankrolled Giaka devalues him as an informant."It makes it easier for somebody to say whatever the person who's giving them money wants them to say," Holt says.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Members of the armed forces collect debris from residential gardens after the mid-air explosion of Pan Am Flight 103I managed to get a hold of the CIA papers - known as cables - from the time, which showed what Giaka had told the Americans.The cables date back to the months before Lockerbie and include notes of conversations between Giaka and Holt and two earlier CIA handlers.Within the cables, Giaka places Megrahi in Malta - where the bomb was said to have been planted - at a key time in the Lockerbie plot.Megrahi is also said to have visited a Maltese clothes shop, buying shirts and baby grows - which were placed in the suitcase with the bomb and later found at the plane crash site.Giaka had even talked to the CIA about eight kilos of orange-coloured explosives stored at the Malta airport offices. Semtex, the explosive used in Lockerbie, is orange.In the 2001 trial, Giaka was to be a "key" witness in the prosecution's case but the four judges de­scribed some of his evidence as "at best grossly ex­ag­ger­ated and at worst sim­ply un­true".The Senussi filesDecades on from Megrahi's conviction, new intelligence documents have been recovered allegedly from the heart of Libyan intelligence.They are believed to have come from Libyan leader Colonel Gaddafi's notorious intelligence network run by his spy chief Abdullah Senussi.These leaked Libyan intelligence documents contain information that could potentially put an end to the doubt, theories and countertheories that have tied so many, including me, in knots.The original 'Senussi Files', as they are now known, were shown to French journalists who later published a book, The Murderer Who Must Be Saved.I travelled to Paris to meet one of the authors, investigative journalist Vincent Nouzille.He brought piles of documents, enough to cover the whole bed and the hotel room desk.You can tell he loves his work and despite having pored over these documents for years, he's still awestruck by their content.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Lockerbie bombing accused Lamin Khalif Fhimah (left) with Libyan leader Colonel Gaddafi after his acquittal in 2001Some of the Senussi files date back to autumn 1988, in the months before Lockerbie, and contain documents apparently detailing plans to target aircraft on multi-stop flights using a 11-hour long-delay timer bomb concealed in luggage much like the Lockerbie bombing.It even mentions tests on concealing a device inside a tape recorder.As we go through each document, my head is spinning.There are references to dry runs, apparent weaknesses in airport security, and enough detail about the movements of Megrahi and others for Nouzille to crosscheck dates and places against other sources.Nouzille says he spent three years carefully verifying everything in the files.He shows me another file which details the apparent movements of Megrahi and Masud, coming in and out of Malta.This account lines up with the information provided in the CIA cables from the previously discredited Giaka."We know from the CIA cables that Giaka reported the same people, the same dates, the same false passport, at the same date," Nouzille says."So two sources, independent, which match."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Abu Agila Masud is accused of making the bomb that blew up Pan Am flight 103 The Senussi Files seem to corroborate several details first mentioned in the cables, including the presence of semtex at Luqa Airport in Malta.Nouzille shows me a translated document, signed by Megrahi, dated January 87, which mentions "10 kilos of explosive material" stored at the airport by Lamin Khalif Fhimah, the man who stood trial alongside Megrahi in 2001 but was acquitted.I tried to contact Fhimah via his trial lawyer to put these allegations to him, but I was unable to reach him.Nouzille concedes that these documents are not "final proof" that Libya was targeting Pan Am 103 flight, but he believes this is evidence of their modus operandi."We have a preparation of a multi-stop flight and a suitcase - and after 11 hours the bomb will explode," Nouzille says.The Senussi Files that Nouzille has are copies, not originals, so they cannot be forensically tested.It remains to be seen whether they will be admissible in the upcoming trial.If they're authentic, these files may prove once and for all that Megrahi was guilty.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Paul Hudson, whose daughter Melina was one of the victims, holds up a banner outside the federal court in Washington DCAs Nouzille packed away the documents, I thought of Jim Swire and what this could all mean for him.He's devoted his life to this case - even befriending Megrahi during his quest to find answers.However, despite the years spent by Nouzille to authenticate the documents, the Senussi Files have failed to convince him that Libya was responsible.Swire says: "I don't think that you should, with your eyes open, go into believing that any documents, however perfect they may seem to be, are genuine which prove conveniently that this was a Libyan job."He said the CIA had the ability to forge any documents they wanted.Despite several delays, Masud is due to go on trial in August this year.Whether this will be pushed back again remains to be seen.It's very likely that historical evidence from the original Lockerbie trial will be brought under the microscope once again - opening up old wounds and catalysing a new era of questioning.Or, if admissible and verified, the Senussi Files might prove once and for all what Dick Marquise and other investigators have been saying all along.

schema.headline: What I learned when I reopened the Lockerbie bombing files

title: Fleeing a wall of flames: Tourists describe France wildfires escape
description: Tourists tell BBC how their holiday turned into race to escape firesImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Evacuation efforts are under way
body: Tourists tell BBC how their holiday turned into race to escape firesImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Evacuation efforts are under way in south-west FranceByEwan SomervilleFamilies have relived how their tranquil holidays in France turned into a race to escape raging wildfires.Tourists told the BBC of emergency alerts in the middle of the night, desperate drives just metres from six-storey high flames and the sight of people flocking to beaches with their suitcases.Huge forest fires in south-west France and central Spain have displaced more than 220,000 people, with the French military drafted in to help and the Spanish government declaring a national emergency.Winds and continued heat are still helping to fan the flames with some tourists reporting smelling acrid smoke like a "bonfire" far outside the affected areas.Flights to Bordeaux and Madrid, the closest cities to the blaze-hit regions, are currently not affected. Earlier on Saturday, a French foreign minister described the fires as a "tragedy" but urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans.Among those caught up in the crisis is Zac Morrison, who arrived in Cap Ferret - a popular peninsula blanketed with pine trees 40 miles (65km) south-west of Bordeaux - on Thursday.The 21-year-old from London, who is on holiday with 10 members of his family, woke up to two text alerts at 04:00 and 06:00 local time ordering him to evacuate "by all means necessary".Image source, Andrea GrettonImage caption, A family showed the BBC how clouds of smoke descended on their campsite in Biscarrosse, south-west France"We had the gendarmerie [French military] going door to door," he told BBC Your Voice. "It was something like out of a movie - we had to take everything."Since experiencing "panic" before a "well organised" operation to clear out the entire peninsula, he said he received four different evacuation alerts from the authorities - the most recent at 17:00 on Friday - after "we moved away from one fire to only get put into the crosshairs of another".His family took shelter on a beach in nearby Arcachon before a relative came to their aid with a place to stay. His brother Nate, 11,  is still coming to terms with having seen the flames."Other people have been sleeping in schools and warehouses and the beaches have had people just waiting for the go ahead," Morrison added. "There's people on the beach here with their suitcases."He said the family was awaiting instructions on whether they can continue their holiday until mid August."It rained last night but we are hearing that electricity may be cut out over the peninsula, especially as the ash clouds go towards Bordeaux... I've heard about houses burning in just an hour, it's scary but sadly people here are getting used to it."Get in touchAre you in an affected region?  If it’s safe to do so, get in touch.Family fled in 15 minutesImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The wildfire on Moutchic beach on the shore of Lake LacanauDavid Morton, a headteacher, had enjoyed most of his week-long trip to Cap Ferret with his wife and two teenage sons in the forests under baking sun. But the mixture of "tinder dry" pine and intense heat helped upend things on day five when the family was awoken on Friday morning."Our phones were all flashing and bleeping; there was a message saying we had to evacuate immediately and drive on the one road out of the [Cap Ferret] peninsula," the 53-year-old said."We literally threw everything into our suitcases and within 15 minutes were in the hire car."He said they came within 500m of the main fire. "The flames were higher than full-size forest pine trees, so five or six storeys high, and it was clear this was a fire that was out of control at that point."The family, from Gloucestershire, has stayed with friends until their flight home from Bordeaux on Saturday.Image source, David MortonImage caption, David Morton's holiday was going smoothly until the final two days'City is evacuated but I'm still here'Others are still stranded. Rebecca Papin, a French-American visiting her holiday home in the commune of Biscarrosse, near to the Cap Ferret peninsula, saw a large plume of smoke in the distance on Thursday.Just three hours later when she arrived home that night, "there were water planes in the sky dropping water, firefighter helicopters in the sky and the entire distance was just a wall of flames," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme."It was quite far away from my house but I could see it very clearly from the upstairs level of my home."She said the authorities appeared "overwhelmed with trying" to fight the fire and issued no evacuation order, so she slept alongside her young children with her earplugs in - meaning she missed the sound of the evacuation overnight.Image source, David MortonImage caption, The flames seen from David Morton's car window"When I woke up in the morning we were almost alone in the city because the city has been evacuated and I'm still here," she said."The main roads are closed because they're on fire - the police advised me on Friday at 07:30 to stay in my home, to not leave my home under any circumstance; there was ash falling from the sky like snow."Some British families told the BBC they had moved 100 miles away to other parts of France to continue their holidays.Mark Dorey, from Leeds, decided to drive to the Dordogne with his wife and three children after being evacuated from a campsite near Parentis-en-Born."You wouldn't believe it, but me and my two boys were watching a Queen tribute act at the campsite bar - straight after a rendition of Bohemian Rhapsody someone stopped them to say we were being evacuated at about 22:00," he said.Image source, Mark DoreyImage caption, Mark Dorey and his family have changed locations in France to complete their holiday with more certaintyBefore heading to the Dordogne the family spent a night with hundreds of other evacuees in a gymnasium.Dorey, 42, said he feels lucky to be looked after and safe, but is thinking about holidaying "closer to home" next year.And BBC South's Joanna Kent, who was on holiday in the Cap Ferret peninsula earlier this week, recalled seeing her campsite deserted after two van loads of police told tourists they had 30 minutes to get out.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Shelters have been set up for evacuated residents and holidaymakersWhile the wildfires show no sign of abating soon, the UK Foreign Office is currently not advising against travel to France or Spain.Éléonore Caroit, France's minister for international partnerships, advised tourists on Saturday: "You have entire areas that are fine, you're seeing similar phenomena in Spain and other countries."I'm in Paris and nothing is happening, and most other regions are OK, so do please come to France and do not cancel your travel plans."But wherever you are, please do be advised as to what might be happening."In Madrid the fires are in the wider region far outside the city centre - and authorities are battling to stop different fires merging.But the flames have already shut down a facility for US space agency Nasa 37 miles (65km) west of the city.Madrid's regional president Isabel Díaz Ayuso described the fire there as the "worst fire in the history of the region", with the area facing a "perfect storm" of high temperatures, relentless wind and merging fire fronts.Additional reporting by: James Kelly, Rozina Sini, Alex Akhurst and Mary Litchfield

schema.headline: Fleeing a wall of flames: Tourists describe France wildfires escape

title: Ormskirk restaurants save day after wedding catering no-show
description: A couple have praised staff at three restaurants that stepped in to save the day when they were let down by wedding caterers at the last minute.Kate a
body: A couple have praised staff at three restaurants that stepped in to save the day when they were let down by wedding caterers at the last minute.Kate and Matt Dean from Skelmersdale, Lancashire, were preparing to celebrate their wedding with family and friends at a venue in Ormskirk when the caterers failed to turn up and they were unable to get in touch with them.With guests starting to arrive, Kate said they decided to ask two local restaurants if they could help.Kate said she first approached restaurant staff at Piri Piri Grill, saying: "Hi! I don't suppose you can cook for 100 people?" and "he just went, 'oh, when?'... and I went, 'now'".The couple, who have four children aged two to 12 between them, were married at Ormskirk Register Office on 13 July.They decided to organise a special celebration for family and friends at Lost and Found Ormskirk on Sunday and were looking forward to the food arriving.They arrived at the venue two hours ahead of time to get it ready but when time was ticking on - with no sign of the caterers - their concern grew.They tried to call and message the business but there was no response and despite initially feeling upset - including crying in the bathroom at one point - Kate quickly hatched a back-up plan."I'm quite a laid back person anyway, so I was in fire-fighting mode, like we have got all these people coming and no food, 'what are we going to do?'," she said.Kate said when guests started arriving she thought about local venues she liked. "I just turned to Matt's family and said, 'if I can sort this, is everybody OK?'"The 32-year-old nail technician said they had been planning their wedding since September, after postman Matt, 36, proposed in 2022.She said the couple approached the teams at Piri Piri Grill and also at Scoozi Pizza and Pasta in Ormskirk and were hugely relieved when they agreed to help out.Despite both restaurants being busy with the World Cup final on that day, they insisted on closing to the public and devoting themselves to helping out the newlyweds, she added.Kate said it was great to see "towers of pizza boxes" which were "taller than Matt and he is 5ft 9ins (1.8m)".Meanwhile, staff at the Lost and Found venue in Ormskirk were "more than accommodating" and "so helpful" in working to ensure the change of plan ran smoothly, she said.Kate said the restaurant staff "were so amazing" and came back later on to check that everything was fine.She said that despite having "ended up crying in the bathroom" at one point, they could see the funny side to what happened as they looked back on the photos."It ended up being quite funny - it was kind of like the wedding story."Their children enjoyed "going around like little waiters with like four pizza boxes" with one saying "you ordered a pizza", she said.

schema.headline: Ormskirk restaurants save day after wedding catering no-show

title: More than 300,000 evacuated as wildfires rage in France and Spain
description: Firefighters are struggling to contain wildfires in south-west France as strong winds push flames towards the city of Bordeaux, with one official sayi
body: Firefighters are struggling to contain wildfires in south-west France as strong winds push flames towards the city of Bordeaux, with one official saying they "are far from having the fire under control."More than 300,000 people in France and Spain have fled fires which have been raging for days, as winds and high temperatures hamper efforts to contain them. In Spain, where a state of emergency has been declared, a change in weather conditions has helped firefighters outside Madrid.Spanish PM Pedro Sánchez admitted there were "complex times ahead". Meanwhile, authorities in València confirmed the death of a man in a fire.The man, believed to be in his 70s, was found dead in his car by firefighters as they extinguished a fire in the Salt de l'Aigua ravine in Manises, according to local media reports.In France, a further 55,000 were ordered to evacuate late on Saturday, taking the total to around 250,000 people in south-western regions of Gironde and Landes regions.Firefighter Captain Nicolas Braz told AFP news agency that the fire had created "its own winds - complete with whirlwinds", adding it was "erratic and unmanageable".It is set to be another "difficult night," he said.France has mobilised its military to help with the response and extra reinforcements from the army have been sent to help firefighters by clearing brush and creating fire breaks.President Emmanuel Macron said France would "rebuild" and his government would "be there for as long as is needed".A British couple holidaying in Bordeaux said they noticed the flames get worse on Friday night, as the fire approached."At about seven o'clock you could smell smoke. We thought someone was having a barbecue," Maisie told BBC Newsbeat from their holiday rental.Her partner, Caleb, said the ash has now covered the pool in the house and turned their feet black when walking outside.The smoke "really hits your lungs right away", they added.Nearby, in Saint-Aubin-de-Médoc, residents evacuating said the situation was "stressful", with one local describing it a "disaster".The final leg of the Tour de France, due to take place Sunday, has been shortened from 133km (83 miles) to 89km (55 miles) so that security forces can be redeployed to areas affected by wildfires, organisers and police have said.Macron is set to have an emergency meeting with ministers as 30 or so fires rage across the country - a situation which the government said is totally unprecedented.She said fires had started earlier in the year when, in April, the Netherlands activated the EU's civil protection mechanism which triggers support and reinforcements from other countries.Lahbib told the BBC: "Last year, one million hectares burned during the summer and so we are expecting to face another historical, sad record because the season has started earlier in the year."She also warned that more outbreaks are likely as the summer goes on. "Forecasters are predicting, unfortunately, another heatwave so we can expect other wildfires," Lahbib added.France has activated the civil protection mechanism and will receive water bombers, comprising three Canadairs planes from Croatia and two Air Tractors from Portugal, as well as Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia, and 40 members of a Romanian forest fire team.EU Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said 11 planes and helicopters have also been sent to France and Spain from the EU's firefighting fleet.Additional reporting by Mary Litchfield, BBC Your Voice and Srosh Khan, BBC Newsbeat

schema.headline: More than 300,000 evacuated as wildfires rage in France and Spain

title: World Matchplay darts 2026 results: Luke Littler and Gerwyn Price reach final in Blackpool
description: Littler has averaged more than 109 in all four matches in this year's tournament as he looks to join Taylor and Michael van Gerwen as the only back-to
body: Littler has averaged more than 109 in all four matches in this year's tournament as he looks to join Taylor and Michael van Gerwen as the only back-to-back winners of the Matchplay.The run is also continuing his sublime form in longer-format matches - this win extending the streak to 28 successive wins in games with 20 or more legs. His last defeat over a match of that duration was when he burst on to the scene in the 2024 World Championship and lost to Luke Humphries in the final.That gives an indication of the challenge that Price will face on Sunday in his second Matchplay final. The pair have a bit of rivalry with Price's on-stage roars and antics often provoking Littler into doing similar, but the teenager denied that Price can get "under his skin".Earlier in the week, Price said that some players can "make it too easy" for Littler. Despite their battles, Littler has won the past nine encounters between the pair, with Price's last success in their opening meeting of 2026. The Welshman has never beat Littler in a game that has contained more than 15 legs so will have to reach new heights in the best-of-35 final. Speaking to Sky Sports, Littler said: "Me and Gez always have great games. Gez will want to try and get me into a roaring battle. As long as I can get into the lead that will be the thing."

schema.headline: World Matchplay darts 2026 results: Luke Littler and Gerwyn Price reach final in Blackpool

title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Adam Ramsay-Peaty in tears after bronze medal
description: After tears in Paris, tears again in Glasgow.It leaves even the great Adam Ramsay-Peaty wondering how much of this is worth it."I work a lot harder th
body: After tears in Paris, tears again in Glasgow.It leaves even the great Adam Ramsay-Peaty wondering how much of this is worth it."I work a lot harder than what it says on the scoreboard," the Englishman said after taking 100m breaststroke bronze at the Commonwealth Games, his eyes and cheeks red with emotion."It hurts too much. I have got to approach training differently now because it hurts too much."Ramsay-Peaty has done it all in this sport.Three Olympic gold medals. Eight world titles. The 14 fastest times in history.But after taking a break from swimming amid a wave of mental health issues in 2023, he is still searching for that winning feeling again on the big stage.He was pipped to Olympic gold in Paris two years ago. In Glasgow, despite coming into the final as the fastest qualifier, he had to settle for bronze.He was beaten by Australia's Sam Williamson but also Jersey's history-maker Filip Nowacki, the 18-year-old he has taken under his wing.Ramsay-Peaty was third at halfway and could not close the gap. His time - 59.65 seconds - was more than four-tenths slower than his semi-final swim and three seconds off his personal best from seven years ago."It took a lot of courage to get back into the sport, so we should be happy with everything we get, but then that contradicts the athlete inside me and what I work for," he said."I just think I deserve more. I know sport isn't about what you deserve or even what you work for - it's who gets it on the day."I just know I'm a better athlete than that. It's very disappointing."Ramsay-Peaty has spoken about the difficult decisions that come with being an elite athlete. The time away from his son, whom he held in his arms after the Paris silver. The events at home he has to miss."They are not even sacrifices; they are choices," he said."It's like getting knocked out in the group stages in the World Cup for a very good team. You know you're better and it hurts because you know you have to wait for a very long time for the next championships."This is probably - realistically - my last Commonwealth Games and I thought I'd trained for better. I could do better. I've been faster this season. That's where the frustration is."Ramsay-Peaty has made no secret of the fact he is still competing in the quest for Olympic gold.He considered retirement again after Paris, but committed to another four years when the 50m race was added to programme for Los Angeles 2028.This 100m breaststroke is his event - the one in which he went unbeaten in eight years - but there may be a time when he has to let it go.The 50m race - a dash down one length of the pool - would be less taxing on the body, and Ramsay-Peaty is due back in the pool for that event on Sunday morning."Is the 100 even viable any more? I don't know," he said."When it hurts like this, the 50 is probably my super strength with my power."With the Olympics, that's probably going to be more realistic, but it's too early to tell."I just feel like I couldn't have given more this cycle. If I had given less, would it have even equalled more?"Given the emotion, there are times you wonder how close Ramsay-Peaty is to walking away entirely.He  appeared to walk to the edge but always turned back, insisting the drive for LA remains."Of course," he said."I know I'm a sprinter. I know I can do very well because I've done it. It doesn't disappear overnight."It requires me to look at the formula and see how I can get to that speed again."

schema.headline: Commonwealth Games 2026: Adam Ramsay-Peaty in tears after bronze medal
